metadata.storyline_summary: The survey opens by profiling the pet household and feeding routine, establishing who the pet is and how the household manages its diet. It then moves through the purchase journey—triggers, channels, frequency, spend, and decision drivers—to reveal how and why they buy. Next, it explores product requirements and trade-offs, including must-haves, quality cues, and price-value expectations, to understand what they want from the food. Finally, it measures satisfaction, friction, and switching risk to identify loyalty and future intent. This arc separates the four segments by their management…
metadata.studyPurpose: Identify which of 4 behavioural segments each pet-owning household belongs to, based on feeding routines, purchase behaviour, and the balance of health, convenience, and price motivations.
metadata.segmentation_lens: Combination of usage/behavioural and jobs-to-be-done: the key axis separating buyers is how they manage their pet's diet (routine vs. actively managed) and what they hire the food to do (basic nutrition, health management, indulgence, or convenience). segments.name: Health-Led Managers Households
segments.description: Households that actively manage their pet's diet for health reasons, often with a vet's input, and are willing to pay a premium for specialized or prescription food. They research ingredients and are loyal to brands that address their pet's specific condition.
segments.hypothesis: This group will report higher spend, more frequent vet consultations, and a strong preference for specialized formats (e.g., prescription, limited-ingredient) over standard dry food.

segments.name: Value-Driven Routine Buyers
segments.description: Households that buy the same food on a regular schedule, prioritizing price and availability over novelty. They are not deeply engaged with ingredients but will switch if the price rises or a coupon appears.
segments.hypothesis: This group will show high purchase frequency, low brand switching, and high price sensitivity, with the majority buying in bulk or on promotion.

segments.name: Convenience-Seeking Subscribers
segments.description: Households that use auto-delivery or online shopping to avoid running out and carrying heavy bags. They value time-saving and reliability over price or ingredient exploration, and are open to trying new brands if the subscription is easy.
segments.hypothesis: This group will report high use of online channels and subscriptions, and will rate convenience and delivery reliability as top decision drivers.

segments.name: Premium Indulgence Owners
segments.description: Households that treat pet food as an extension of care and pampering, choosing premium, natural, or eco-friendly options regardless of cost. They are influenced by branding, ingredient stories, and sustainability claims.
segments.hypothesis: This group will show low price sensitivity, high engagement with premium claims, and a willingness to pay more for perceived quality and ethical production.

segmentModel.tie_break: Question cp7 (main goal when choosing pet food) is the most direct behavioural self-report because it forces respondents to state their primary motivation, cleanly separating health management, value, convenience, and natural/premium indulgence.
notes: Weights are assigned only to options that clearly discriminate between segments; neutral or common options are left unscored.
Each segment has at least two scoring options and at least one 3-point option.
Some options like 'Other' or generic 'My pet will eat it' are not scored because they do not discriminate.
The duplicate question bb4 was not scored to avoid double counting.
segmentModel.excluded: Screening and Profiling questions are excluded from scoring: screeners carry no signal (everyone passed) and demographics are for cross-tabs, not segmentation.

fieldingNotes.recommendedSample: n=800-1,200 for stable segment-level sub-groups (roughly n>=312 per segment after weighting). At n=1,000 the margin of error on a whole-sample percentage is about ±3.1pp at 95% confidence; on a segment of n=200 it widens to about ±6.9pp, so segment-level differences under ~10pp should not be reported as real.
fieldingNotes.quotaControls: Apply quotas on the category-usage and frequency screeners so heavy users — who are more willing survey-takers — are not over-sampled.
scriptingNotes: Rotate the order of answer options on every non-ordinal question to remove primacy bias. Do NOT rotate ordinal scales (frequency bands, price bands, satisfaction) — their order carries meaning.
Anchor 'Other', 'None of these' and 'Prefer not to say' to the bottom of the list, exempt from rotation.
Every 'Other' option takes an open-text capture, coded back into the frame at analysis if any single verbatim exceeds 3%.
No routing or skip logic: every respondent sees every question, so the base is constant across the instrument.
Include one attention check in the middle third — a standard instructed-response item. Terminate on failure and replace.
Randomise the order of the two ranking/trade-off items between respondents so neither is systematically answered while fresher.
caveats: Percentages in this document are simulated from a persona-weighted panel, not fielded with real respondents. Replace with primary data after fielding.
Ranking items are shown as a lighter-weight ranking exercise; run them as MaxDiff if you need more precision on driver importance.
Profiling questions are for cross-tabs only and are excluded from the segmentation scoring model.
